title: Chat application
scopeHtml:
Scope: 1:1 and group rooms, observer delivery, mediator service, per-room ordering.

Scope: 1:1 and group rooms, observer delivery, mediator service, per-room ordering.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design the LLD of a chat application: register users, send 1:1 and group messages, deliver them to members, and fetch recent history. Network transport (WebSockets) is out of scope; we model the objects and the delivery logic.

Clarify:

  • Functional: 1:1 chat, group chat, message history (last N), only members may post.
  • Not now: media, read receipts, end-to-end encryption, presence.
  • Scale talk: WhatsApp reported around 100 billion messages a day; a single group is at most a few hundred (WhatsApp cap was 1,024 members at the time of writing, confirm current). Per-conversation logic is small; the system is hard because of fan-out and connections.

Worked example. A group of 200 members and 1 message per second per active group: 199 deliveries per second for that one group. 10,000 such groups is about 2M deliveries per second, which is why real systems shard by conversation.

Industry examples. WhatsApp runs Erlang servers holding millions of connections each; Slack and Discord model everything as a channel, and a DM is a channel of two. Kafka or similar logs store ordered messages per conversation.

Everyday analogy. A notice board per room: anything pinned is copied into each member's pigeonhole.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing separate code paths for 1:1 and group.
  • Skipping the membership check.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• User (name, inbox, implements listener).
  • ChatRoom (id, members, history). A 1:1 chat is a room of two.
  • Message (id, from, text, timestamp); immutable record.
  • ChatService: registers users, creates rooms, sends, reads history.

Decision gravity. "1:1 is a 2-member room" removes a whole class of duplicate code. Reversible: yes. The room id for a pair is the sorted pair of names so direct(a, b) and direct(b, a) return the same room.

Everyday analogy. A DM is just a very small group.

Common interview traps.

  • Two different message tables or classes for DM and group.
  • Message ids from System.currentTimeMillis(); they collide. Use a sequence.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+-------------+  *   * +-----------+ 1    * +-----------+
| User        |<-------| ChatRoom  |------->| Message   |
| name        | members| id        |history | id from   |
| inbox       |        +-----------+        | text ts   |
+-------------+                             +-----------+
      ^ implements
<<ChatListener>> onMessage(room, msg)

ChatService: register, createGroup, direct, send, lastN

Common interview traps.

  • Making Message mutable so a later edit rewrites history.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Observer: users implement ChatListener; the room pushes each message to every member. In production the listener is a WebSocket connection or a push-notification (FCM/APNs) sender.
  • Mediator: ChatService and ChatRoom sit between users so users never hold references to each other. Alternative: users call each other, which creates a mesh of N squared links.
  • Immutable value object for Message.
  • Reversible: yes. The one-way door is the message id and ordering scheme once data is stored.

Worked example. asha posts to "team" (asha, ben, cy): ben and cy get it, asha does not get her own echo. Output shows cy's inbox [team] asha: standup now.

Industry examples. Slack fans out via a pub/sub per channel; Discord uses per-guild state and Elixir/Erlang style processes; WhatsApp stores messages on the server only until delivery.

Everyday analogy. A post office (mediator): you hand letters to it, never to each recipient.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending to the sender too.
  • Letting users be notified before the message is stored (a crash then loses it).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;

record Message(long id, String from, String text, long ts) {}

interface ChatListener { void onMessage(String room, Message m); }

class User implements ChatListener {
    final String name; final List<String> inbox = new ArrayList<>();
    User(String n) { name = n; }
    public void onMessage(String room, Message m) { inbox.add("[" + room + "] " + m.from() + ": " + m.text()); }
}

class ChatRoom {
    final String id; final Map<String, User> members = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    final List<Message> history = new ArrayList<>();
    ChatRoom(String id) { this.id = id; }
}

class ChatService {
    private final Map<String, User> users = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, ChatRoom> rooms = new HashMap<>();
    private long seq = 0;

    User register(String name) { return users.computeIfAbsent(name, User::new); }

    ChatRoom createGroup(String id, String... names) {
        ChatRoom r = new ChatRoom(id);
        for (String n : names) r.members.put(n, users.get(n));
        rooms.put(id, r); return r;
    }
    ChatRoom direct(String a, String b) {          // 1:1 is just a 2-member room
        String id = a.compareTo(b) < 0 ? a + "|" + b : b + "|" + a;
        ChatRoom r = rooms.get(id);
        return r != null ? r : createGroup(id, a, b);
    }
    void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
        ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
        if (!r.members.containsKey(from)) throw new SecurityException("not a member");
        Message m = new Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
        r.history.add(m);
        for (User u : r.members.values()) if (!u.name.equals(from)) u.onMessage(roomId, m);
    }
    List<Message> lastN(String roomId, int n) {
        List<Message> h = rooms.get(roomId).history;
        return h.subList(Math.max(0, h.size() - n), h.size());
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ChatService s = new ChatService();
        User a = s.register("asha"), b = s.register("ben"), c = s.register("cy");
        s.register("zed");
        s.createGroup("team", "asha", "ben", "cy");
        s.send("team", "asha", "standup now");
        ChatRoom d = s.direct("ben", "asha");
        s.send(d.id, "ben", "ok coming");
        System.out.println(a.inbox); System.out.println(c.inbox);
        try { s.send("team", "zed", "hi"); throw new AssertionError(); }
        catch (SecurityException e) { System.out.println("blocked non-member"); }
        System.out.println(s.lastN("team", 5).size());
    }
}

Kotlin core:

data class Message(val id: Long, val from: String, val text: String, val ts: Long)

class User(val name: String) {
    val inbox = mutableListOf<String>()
    fun onMessage(room: String, m: Message) { inbox += "[$room] ${m.from}: ${m.text}" }
}

class ChatRoom(val id: String, val members: Map<String, User>) {
    val history = mutableListOf<Message>()
}

class ChatService {
    private val users = mutableMapOf<String, User>()
    private val rooms = mutableMapOf<String, ChatRoom>()
    private var seq = 0L
    fun register(n: String) = users.getOrPut(n) { User(n) }
    fun createGroup(id: String, vararg names: String) =
        ChatRoom(id, names.associateWith { users.getValue(it) }).also { rooms[id] = it }
    fun send(roomId: String, from: String, text: String) {
        val r = rooms.getValue(roomId)
        require(from in r.members) { "not a member" }
        val m = Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis())
        r.history += m                                    // store first, then deliver
        r.members.values.filter { it.name != from }.forEach { it.onMessage(roomId, m) }
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing storage and delivery so a slow user blocks others.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
[[asha|ben] ben: ok coming]
[[team] asha: standup now]
blocked non-member
1

Test: non-member rejected, no echo to sender, direct(a,b) equals direct(b,a), lastN with N larger than history.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing that order is preserved.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Problems in the simple version: seq increments race (duplicate ids), history (ArrayList) is corrupted by concurrent adds, and a slow listener blocks the sender.

Thread-safe version.

class ChatRoom {
    final Map<String, User> members = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<Message> history = new ArrayList<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // per room: order within a room

    Message append(String from, String text, AtomicLong ids) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Message m = new Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
            history.add(m);                    // order of history == order of ids inside this room
            return m;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

// delivery is OUTSIDE the lock, on an executor
void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
    Message m = r.append(from, text, ids);
    for (User u : r.members.values())
        if (!u.name.equals(from)) pool.execute(() -> u.onMessage(roomId, m));
}

The per-room lock guarantees one total order per conversation, which is the guarantee users actually notice. Global ordering across rooms is not needed. User inbox should be a ConcurrentLinkedQueue.

Production note (gravity). Distributed: one conversation maps to one shard/partition (Kafka key = room id) so a single consumer orders it. Choosing the partition key is a one-way door. Delivery is at-least-once, so clients dedupe by message id.

Common interview traps.

  • A single global lock for the whole service.
  • Delivering while holding the room lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Offline users: store undelivered messages, deliver on reconnect (queue per user).
  • Read receipts and typing: more event types on the same Observer.
  • Pagination: history(before=id, limit=50).
  • Mute, block, admin roles: permission check in send.
  • Search: inverted index per room.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising exactly-once delivery; say at-least-once plus dedupe.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• 1:1 chat is a 2-member room; one code path.
  • Observer for delivery, mediator service in the middle, immutable messages.
  • Store first, then deliver; never echo to sender.
  • Thread safety: per-room lock for ordering, atomic ids, deliver outside the lock.
  • At scale: shard by conversation, at-least-once with client dedupe.

questions.promptHtml: In a chat LLD, why would you model a 1:1 chat as a room with two members instead of a separate DirectChat class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you remove duplicate code paths by choosing the right abstraction, and whether you think about identity of a pair.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A DM is just a very small group. If I model both as ChatRoom with a member set, send, history, membership check and delivery are written once. The only 1:1-specific part is the room id: I build it from the sorted pair of names so direct(a,b) and direct(b,a) return the same room.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two classes means two history stores, two send paths, two sets of bugs, and every new feature (mute, pagination, receipts) is built twice. Slack and Discord do the same: a DM is a channel of two.

direct("ben","asha") -> id = "asha|ben"   (sorted)
direct("asha","ben") -> id = "asha|ben"   (same room, found in map)

If the id were "a|b" in argument order you would silently create two rooms and each person would see half the conversation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
ChatRoom direct(String a, String b) {
    String id = a.compareTo(b) < 0 ? a + "|" + b : b + "|" + a;
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(id);
    return r != null ? r : createGroup(id, a, b);
}
fun direct(a: String, b: String): ChatRoom {
    val id = if (a < b) "$a|$b" else "$b|$a"
    return rooms[id] ?: createGroup(id, a, b)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Separate tables or classes for DM and group.
  • Unsorted pair id, so two rooms exist for one pair.
  • Using a name containing the separator ("a|b") as a user name; real systems use user ids.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a user can be renamed? -> Key by immutable user id, not name.
  2. What if a DM must later become a group? -> Create a new room with the three members; do not mutate the pair id.
  3. Is direct safe under concurrent calls? -> No, two threads can both miss and create; use computeIfAbsent on a ConcurrentHashMap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "less code". Senior also names the id-canonicalisation rule, the race in get-or-create, and that the pair-id scheme is the one-way door once data is stored.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped DM ids in argument order; support tickets said "my messages vanished", which were really two rooms.

questions.promptHtml: Which design patterns are in a chat system and what does each one buy you? Why not let users hold references to each other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks pattern vocabulary tied to concrete consequences, not name-dropping.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Observer: each User implements ChatListener and the room pushes every message to it. Mediator: ChatService and ChatRoom sit in the middle so no user knows another user. Without the mediator, N users need N*(N-1) links, and adding a member means updating everyone. Message is an immutable value object so nobody can rewrite history.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mesh (no mediator)          Mediator
A <-> B <-> C               A -> Room -> B
 ^----------^                      -> C
links: N(N-1)               links: N

In production the listener is a WebSocket session or an FCM/APNs sender, so the Observer interface is exactly the seam where "in-memory inbox" is swapped for "network push". The room does not care which one.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it Observer but making users poll.
  • Letting the listener throw and abort delivery to the remaining members.
  • Mutable Message, so an edit rewrites what others already saw.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the Observer interface bite? -> Slow or failing listener; you need isolation per listener (executor, try/catch).
  2. Could ChatRoom be the mediator without ChatService? -> Yes for delivery; the service adds registry and room lookup.
  3. How would typing indicators and receipts fit? -> More event types on the same listener, not new patterns.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names the patterns. Senior says what breaks (slow listener, fan-out cost) and that both are reversible while the message id scheme is not.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One crashing push-sender listener used to stop delivery to everyone after it in the loop until each call got its own try/catch.

questions.contextHtml:
A reviewer finds this in ChatService and says there are two bugs that only appear in production:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
    Message m = new Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
    for (User u : r.members.values()) u.onMessage(roomId, m);   // delivers first
    r.history.add(m);
}
List<Message> lastN(String roomId, int n) {
    List<Message> h = rooms.get(roomId).history;
    return h.subList(Math.max(0, h.size() - n), h.size());
}
fun send(roomId: String, from: String, text: String) {
    val r = rooms.getValue(roomId)
    val m = Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis())
    r.members.values.forEach { it.onMessage(roomId, m) }   // delivers first
    r.history += m
}
fun lastN(roomId: String, n: Int) = rooms.getValue(roomId).history.takeLast(n)

An API handler iterates the result of lastN while another thread sends a message. Users report "I got a notification but the message is not in history" after a crash.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots only the echo or the missing membership check. Misses the ordering of store versus notify, and that subList is a live view.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the history in memory or a DB? Is delivery best-effort or guaranteed? Are listeners remote (slow)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reorder: append to history first, then deliver.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deliver-before-store loses a message that users already saw if the process crashes in between; (b) no membership check and the sender gets an echo; (c) the Java subList is a view over the ArrayList; a concurrent add makes iteration throw ConcurrentModificationException; (d) ++seq is not atomic.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test with a listener that throws, then assert history contains the message; a test that iterates lastN result while another thread sends; kill -9 test between the two steps.
  5. Root cause: Delivery has an external effect (the user has seen it); storage is the source of truth, so it must happen first. subList returns a window on mutable shared state.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
    if (!r.members.containsKey(from)) throw new SecurityException("not a member");
    Message m = new Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
    r.history.add(m);                                           // store first
    for (User u : r.members.values()) if (!u.name.equals(from)) u.onMessage(roomId, m);
}
List<Message> lastN(String roomId, int n) {
    List<Message> h = rooms.get(roomId).history;
    return List.copyOf(h.subList(Math.max(0, h.size() - n), h.size()));   // snapshot
}
fun send(roomId: String, from: String, text: String) {
    val r = rooms.getValue(roomId)
    require(from in r.members) { "not a member" }
    val m = Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis())
    r.history += m
    r.members.values.filter { it.name != from }.forEach { it.onMessage(roomId, m) }
}
fun lastN(roomId: String, n: Int) = rooms.getValue(roomId).history.takeLast(n).toList()
  1. Prevention: A test that a throwing listener still leaves the message stored; a lint/review rule "never return a live view of internal state".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap everything in one global lock to hide the race; the copy is O(n) for small n and cheap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Crash after store, before delivery? -> Message is in history; recipients get it on reconnect from the pending queue or by fetching since last seen id.
  • Why not copy the whole history? -> Only the last N are needed; copy just that window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A notification service fired pushes before the DB commit; a rollback then left users holding a push for a message that never existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only finds the echo/membership issue.
  • Hire: finds store-before-notify and the subList view.
  • Strong hire: also names atomic ids, recovery after crash, and writes the test for each.

questions.subtopic: requirement change, offline users and mute
questions.contextHtml: The system works with always-online users. Product now asks for two things in one sprint: (1) users who are offline must receive messages when they reconnect; (2) a user can mute a room (no push, but still stored) and block another user in DMs. About 5% of 500,000 users are offline at any moment.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which stay the same, and where does each new rule live?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (offline) and if (muted) branches inside ChatRoom.send, so the room now knows about presence and preferences.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max backlog per user and TTL? Does muted still count unread? Is block symmetric? Do blocked users see the block?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, it is feature work; I start with the smallest slice: pending queue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) branches in the room, (b) a DeliveryPolicy or listener decorator, (c) per-user Inbox abstraction that is either live or queued.
  4. How I'd verify each: Which option keeps ChatRoom unchanged when the next rule arrives (open/closed)?
  5. Root cause: Delivery is the variable part. Offline queueing is a property of the listener: PendingListener wraps the real listener and buffers while disconnected; muting is a check in the listener or a MutePolicy. The room still just loops over listeners.
  6. Fix: New classes: Presence (or connection state), PendingQueue per user, MuteSettings. Changed: User gains a state; ChatService.send unchanged except it calls deliver(user, msg). Blocking is a permission check in send for DMs. On reconnect: drain queue ordered by message id, dedupe by id on the client.
  7. Prevention: Tests: offline then online gets messages in order exactly once; muted user gets nothing live but lastN has it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not put the queue in memory only for real; a crash loses it. I would not store a copy of the text per offline user; store message ids and fetch from history.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backlog grows unbounded for a user offline for a month? -> Cap and fall back to "fetch history since last seen id".
  • Muted group with @mention? -> Policy returns "deliver" for mentions; another rule, same seam.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chat product added mute by filtering in the push sender only; unread badges still counted muted rooms, because the rule lived in one of three places.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: if/else in send.
  • Hire: decorator or policy at the listener seam.
  • Strong hire: ids not copies, ordered drain, dedupe, and bounded backlog.

questions.contextHtml: Your ChatService creates User objects itself and delivery writes to an in-memory inbox string list. QA wants tests for: no echo to sender, non-member rejected, order preserved, and "one failing listener does not block the others". Another engineer says "we need Mockito and a real WebSocket server".
questions.promptHtml: How do you make this testable and what do the tests look like?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts a real network server in the test or sleeps and prints inboxes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the listener interface already separate? Do we have a place to inject the id generator and clock?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Depend on the ChatListener interface only; register a recording fake.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: What makes tests flaky: real time, real threads, real network.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fake listener records (room, msg); a throwing fake for the isolation test; inject LongSupplier clock and id sequence.
  5. Root cause: Hard-wired concrete User and System.currentTimeMillis() make behaviour untestable.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Recording implements ChatListener {
    final List<Message> got = new ArrayList<>();
    public void onMessage(String room, Message m) { got.add(m); }
}
class Boom implements ChatListener {
    public void onMessage(String room, Message m) { throw new RuntimeException("down"); }
}
// test: sender receives nothing, member receives once, Boom does not stop others
class Recording : ChatListener {
    val got = mutableListOf<Message>()
    override fun onMessage(room: String, m: Message) { got += m }
}
class Boom : ChatListener {
    override fun onMessage(room: String, m: Message) = throw RuntimeException("down")
}
  1. Prevention: Test list: non-member rejected, no echo, direct(a,b) == direct(b,a), lastN with N larger than history, ids strictly increasing, order of 100 messages preserved, one throwing listener still leaves others served.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No Thread.sleep asserts; with an executor, use a latch or a direct executor in tests. I would keep one thin integration test for the real transport.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test the concurrent path? -> Many threads send, then assert ids unique and history order equals id order per room.
  • Mock vs fake? -> Fake for a simple recording interface; mocks for verifying call counts only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A suite using real sleeps took 9 minutes and failed one run in ten; swapping in a fake clock and direct executor made it 4 seconds and deterministic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tests via the network.
  • Hire: fake listener, isolation test.
  • Strong hire: also injects time and executor and tests per-room order concurrently.

questions.contextHtml:
Two threads send to the same room at nearly the same time. Users report that in a group of 50, some clients show message 41 before message 40, and the history API once returned two messages with id 87. The code:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long seq = 0;
void send(String roomId, String from, String text) {
    ChatRoom r = rooms.get(roomId);
    Message m = new Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
    r.history.add(m);            // ArrayList
    deliver(r, m);
}
var seq = 0L
fun send(roomId: String, from: String, text: String) {
    val r = rooms.getValue(roomId)
    val m = Message(++seq, from, text, System.currentTimeMillis())
    r.history += m               // ArrayList
    deliver(r, m)
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failures and give a correct design. Do you need a global lock?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make send synchronized" without saying why that is too coarse, or "use ConcurrentHashMap" which does nothing for ++seq or the list.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering required globally or per conversation? Is history in memory? How many rooms are hot?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A per-room ReentrantLock around id assignment plus history append.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ++seq is read-modify-write, two threads read 86 and both write 87; (b) ArrayList.add is not thread-safe, can lose or corrupt entries; (c) id order differs from append order because the two steps are not atomic together.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress test with 8 threads x 10,000 sends: assert ids unique and history.get(i).id < history.get(i+1).id.
  5. Root cause: The invariant "history order equals id order within a room" spans two operations, so each needs a common critical section.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Message append(String from, String text, AtomicLong ids) {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        Message m = new Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis());
        history.add(m);
        return m;
    } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
// deliver OUTSIDE the lock
fun append(from: String, text: String, ids: AtomicLong): Message = lock.withLock {
    Message(ids.incrementAndGet(), from, text, System.currentTimeMillis()).also { history += it }
}
  1. Prevention: The stress test in CI; a code rule that history is private and mutated only through append.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No global lock: users only notice per-conversation order, and a global lock serialises unrelated rooms. I would not deliver while holding the room lock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could ids be per-room counters instead of a global AtomicLong? -> Yes under the room lock, and it avoids a shared hot counter; ids become unique per (room, seq).
  • Does the lock fix delivery order at clients? -> It fixes append order; delivery on an executor can still reorder, so deliver per room via a single-threaded queue or let clients sort by id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A group chat sorted by client receive time showed replies before the question; sorting by the server-assigned room sequence fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronized on the service, no reasoning.
  • Hire: per-room lock, atomic id, delivery outside.
  • Strong hire: separates append order from delivery order and proposes a stress test.

questions.subtopic: slow listener in a large group
questions.contextHtml:
A 1,000-member company announcement room. Post-deploy, p99 of send jumps from 8 ms to 4.5 s and other rooms get slow too. Thread dump shows 200 request threads in ChatService.send, many BLOCKED on one ReentrantLock owned by a thread inside User.onMessage -> PushClient.post. Push provider latency is up from 20 ms to 400 ms. CPU is 15%, heap is fine, DB is healthy.

"http-17" holds <0x7f3a> room-lock(announce)
  at PushClient.post(...)
  at User.onMessage(...)
  at ChatService.deliver(...)
  at ChatService.send(...)
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What do you do first, and what do you change in the design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases thread pool size or the timeout. Blames the push provider only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is delivery inside the lock in code? Are other rooms slow because they share a pool or because the lock is global? Is the push call retried?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag push for that room off or set a 200 ms client timeout; the message is stored, users still get it on next poll.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) delivery runs under the room lock, so one slow call holds it 1,000 x 0.4 s; (b) shared request pool exhausted by blocked threads, hitting other rooms; (c) provider degradation is only the trigger.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack shows owner thread inside PushClient.post; lock hold time metric; pool active-thread gauge at max.
  5. Root cause: Slow external I/O executed inside the critical section that only needed to cover id and append. 1,000 sequential remote calls at 400 ms is 400 s of lock-holding in the worst case.
  6. Fix: Short term: release the lock before deliver, timeouts and try/catch per listener. Long term: hand each message to a delivery executor (or per-user outbound queue) with a bounded queue, parallel fan-out and metrics.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Message m = r.append(from, text, ids);              // lock held only here
for (User u : r.members.values())
    if (!u.name.equals(from)) pool.execute(() -> safeDeliver(u, roomId, m));
val m = r.append(from, text, ids)                    // lock held only here
r.members.values.filter { it.name != from }
    .forEach { u -> pool.execute { safeDeliver(u, roomId, m) } }
  1. Prevention: Alert on lock wait time and push p99; bulkhead pools per concern; a test with a listener that sleeps 2 s proving send returns fast.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just grow the pool; that moves the collapse. Async delivery means at-least-once with retries, so clients dedupe by message id.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The delivery queue fills up? -> Bounded queue; drop push (not storage) and rely on pull-on-open; apply back-pressure per room.
  • Order of delivery to one user? -> Use a per-user serial queue so a retry does not reorder.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A broadcast feature held a mutex across 3,000 webhook calls; the first slow partner took the whole product's posting path down.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes pool and timeout only.
  • Hire: moves delivery outside the lock and adds timeouts.
  • Strong hire: bulkheads, bounded queues, at-least-once with dedupe, and explicit mitigation before the fix.

questions.contextHtml: The single-process chat works for 20,000 concurrent users. Target: 2M concurrent users, 1.5M messages/min peak (about 25,000/s), largest room 1,000 members, average room 8. A teammate proposes "one global Kafka topic, 3 partitions, key = sender id, exactly-once delivery".
questions.promptHtml: Critique the proposal and give your design for ordering and delivery.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts it, or says "just add more servers" and ignores ordering.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What ordering do users need (per conversation)? Max acceptable delivery latency? Loss tolerance? Is history durable server-side?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would first state the guarantees: per-conversation total order, at-least-once, idempotent clients.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Wrong choices in the proposal: (a) key by sender breaks per-room order since two senders in one room land on different partitions; (b) 3 partitions caps parallelism; (c) exactly-once end to end to a phone is not achievable, the last hop is a network.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reason about throughput: 25,000 msg/s x avg 8 members = about 200,000 deliveries/s; the large rooms add skew.
  5. Root cause: The ordering unit is the conversation, so the partition key must be the room id. That choice is a one-way door once data is stored.
  6. Fix: Key = room id, many partitions (hundreds, verify per cluster sizing). One consumer owns a partition, runs the same append-and-deliver logic. Gateways hold connections; delivery looks up which gateway holds each member. Clients dedupe by (room, seq).
  7. Prevention: Load test with a skewed room distribution; metric on partition lag; per-room hot-key alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise exactly-once; I would promise at-least-once plus dedupe. A 1,000-member room is hot but bounded; a 100,000-member channel needs a different (pull/fan-out-on-read) model.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A partition's consumer dies? -> Rebalance; another consumer resumes from the committed offset; clients dedupe replays.
  • Re-partitioning later? -> Painful because room-to-partition mapping changes; plan partition count up front or use a mapping layer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team keyed their stream by user id; conversations arrived out of order only under load, which made it a one-in-a-thousand bug nobody could reproduce locally.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the proposal or "add servers".
  • Hire: keys by room, says at-least-once with dedupe.
  • Strong hire: does the fan-out math, handles hot rooms, and names the key choice as a one-way door.
